Floriculture: A Blossoming Industry

The science and art of growing flowering and ornamental plants, with healthy soil, proper irrigation, careful plant care and sustainable practices that benefit the community.

🌹 🌺 🌼 🪻 🌸

About the project

This is the community service project of four B.Tech Computer Science and Engineering students from Sree Venkateswara College of Engineering, Nellore. From 01 June to 26 July 2026 we worked with the floriculture community of B.V. Nagar, Nellore, where flower growing is the main livelihood of many households.

We met floriculturists, nursery practitioners and elderly growers, visited a nursery and a greenhouse, surveyed sixteen flowering and ornamental plants, and held an awareness programme on marketing, financial planning and the benefits of floriculture as a business.

Community

B.V. Nagar, Nellore, Andhra Pradesh

8 weeks: 01-06-2026 to 26-07-2026

Each day of fieldwork we studied one plant: how it is grown, where it is used and how to handle it safely.

Safety note: oleander is highly toxic, and the sap of allamanda and alocasia irritates skin. Traditional remedies mentioned in our survey should only be used under expert guidance.

Mini project: grafting in floriculture

Grafting joins parts of two plants so they grow as one. The scion is the upper part that becomes the shoot system, and the rootstock is the lower part that becomes the root system. Growers graft to improve disease resistance, raise yield and combine the best traits of different plants.

When to graft

Usually in the dormant season, late winter or early spring, so the graft union can heal before active growth begins. Exact timing depends on the species and local climate, so check with local gardening experts.

Tools you need

Cutting tools

Sharp, clean knives (bud-grafting, pruning), plus saws and chisels for large stock.

Disinfectant

Alcohol is the most common agent for keeping the site free of pathogens.

Tying materials

Strips, twine, nails and splints, often dampened, hold scion and stock together.

Graft seals

Clay, wax, petroleum jelly or tape keep the site moist but allow growth.

The process

  1. Stem grafting: a shoot of the desired cultivar is grafted onto the stock of another plant.
  2. Bud grafting: a dormant side bud is grafted onto the stock stem. Once it has joined (inosculated), the stock above the bud is pruned to encourage growth.
  3. Common methods include whip and tongue, chip budding, cleft grafting and T budding.

Factors for success

Compatibility

The closer two plants are genetically, the likelier the union. Monocots lack vascular cambium and normally cannot be grafted.

Right age and season

Graft while the scion is dormant. Too warm causes premature budding; too cold slows callus formation.

Cambium alignment

Press the cambium layers tightly together in the direction of normal growth.

Aftercare

Seal against water loss, support the joint, and prune rootstock shoots that crowd the scion.

Our recommendations

  • Graft in the dormant season.
  • Choose scion and rootstock that are genetically close.
  • Sharpen and disinfect tools before each use.
  • Seal the graft with tape or wax and provide proper aftercare.

Problems we found in the community

Heat, cold and erratic rainNutrient-poor or compacted soilOver- and under-wateringAphids, mites, mildew, root rot

Short-term fixes: add compost, use drip irrigation, apply eco-friendly pest control. Long-term: regular workshops, integrated pest management training and partnerships with agricultural institutions.
